summary: For ages 8–11, learners run the engineering test→find failure point→improve→retest loop on a prototype (bridge, parachute, boat). The core skill is controlled fair testing of a model: hold every condition constant except the one design feature being changed, locate the SPECIFIC point where and why it fails, propose an improvement targeted at that failure, and retest under identical conditions so any gain can be credited to the change. Hands-on building and testing is the primary vehicle (consistent with the KS2/NGSS requirement for pupils to build, test and improve); build-and-test simulations, a 3D structure sandbox, a reference diagram, recognition checks and a design-mentor dialogue serve as distinct supports with their own purposes and limits.
misconceptions: Treating a test as a pass/fail verdict rather than as diagnostic information about where and why the design failed.
Changing several design features at once between versions, then not knowing which change produced the improvement (loss of fair-test control).
Believing a first failure means the design (or the designer) is 'wrong', rather than that iteration is the normal engineering process.
Proposing improvements based on appearance or preference instead of on the observed failure point.
Judging a prototype on a single trial, ignoring that variability needs repeat runs to see the real behaviour.

activities.title: Build, test, and diagnose the failure point of a prototype
steps: Build a simple prototype against stated design criteria — e.g. a paper bridge spanning the gap between two tables, a parachute, or a floating boat.

Plan a fair test: decide one loading/testing method and keep it fixed (same weight increments, same position, same drop height), and agree that version 2 will change only one design feature, chosen after you see where and how version 1 fails.

Run the test and observe carefully WHERE and HOW it fails — e.g. 'it sagged and tore in the middle', 'the seam leaked at the corner', 'it buckled near the left support'. Record this failure point, not just pass/fail.
Propose one specific improvement aimed squarely at that failure point (e.g. 'it snapped in the middle, so I'll add a support there' or 'fold the middle to stiffen it').
Build version 2 changing only that one feature, then retest under identical conditions, and judge from the results whether it actually improved.
activities.insight: A test is a diagnosis, not a verdict: it shows where and how the design failed, giving evidence for reasoning about why, so you know what to change. Changing only one feature between versions, while keeping test conditions identical, is what lets you credit an improvement to that change (repeat trials then check it was not a fluke).

activities.title: Repeat trials and quantify before crediting an improvement
steps: For one prototype version, run the same test several times (repeat trials), using a fresh identical copy whenever the test destroys the prototype, and record the measured outcome each time — mass held, distance travelled, drop time.
Compare the repeat results: notice whether a single run was a fluke or whether the behaviour is consistent.
Fill in a version-comparison table: v1 vs v2, the single changed feature, and the measured outcome for each, with repeat trials for each version.
Decide whether version 2 is genuinely better given the spread of results, not just one lucky run.
activities.insight: A fragile prototype's result shouldn't be judged on a single run; repeat trials and measurement reveal the real behaviour and make an 'improvement' claim trustworthy.

activities.title: Build-and-test simulation with a locked version tray (supporting scaffold)
steps: In a bridge/parachute/boat builder with a test rig, assemble a prototype and load/drop/float it under fixed conditions.
When it fails, read the overlay that highlights the exact failure point (the beam that buckles, the seam that leaks) and name where and why it failed.
Use a version tray that keeps v1 beside v2 and locks all conditions except the one feature you change; reinforce precisely the highlighted failure point and retest.
Watch whether the prototype survives the identical retest, and connect that result to the single change you made.
activities.insight: Seeing the exact failure point highlighted and retesting under locked identical conditions can make 'test as diagnosis' and 'controlled comparison' visible and fast to iterate.

activities.title: 3D structure sandbox for inherently spatial failure modes (alternative)
steps: For a structure whose failure is genuinely three-dimensional (buckling, twisting, toppling of a bridge, tower or parachute), build it in a 3D builder with physics and load it.
Observe how it deforms and fails in three dimensions, which a flat side view might hide.
Target the spatial weakness (e.g. add bracing against twist), then retest under identical conditions.
activities.insight: Some failure modes are spatial, so viewing deformation in three dimensions can reveal a weakness that a single 2D view may not show.

activities.title: Recognition checks and design-mentor dialogue (recognition and justification supports)
steps: Answer a multiple-choice item: 'Which version comparison is a fair test?' (only one design feature differs between versions and the test conditions are identical).
Match observed failure points to the improvement that targets each one.
Put the test–improve–retest steps into the correct order.
After testing, defend your change to a design-mentor who asks 'what's your evidence that this will fix it?' and justify the improvement from the test observation.
activities.insight: Learners can check that they recognise fair comparisons, the evidence→improvement link and the iteration loop, and can articulate the reasoning behind a change — though recognising a fair test is not the same as producing one at the bench.

checkQuestion: Here's a paper bridge you've built spanning two tables, and some weights. Plan and run a fair test to find out how much it holds, spot where and why it fails, then make one improvement and test again to see if it's better. Keep the test fair each time. I'll watch.
checkAnswer: The child loads the bridge in a controlled way (same position, same weight increments), identifies the specific failure point and why it fails (e.g. it sags and tears in the middle), makes a targeted change aimed at that weakness (e.g. folds or beams the middle), and retests under identical conditions so the before/after comparison is fair — then judges whether it actually improved.
